title: Indigenous people were here first
text: Indigenous people lived here long before there was a city. For thousands of years this was their land: the Huron-Wendat, the Haudenosaunee and the Anishinaabe, including the Mississaugas of the Credit. The name Toronto comes from a Mohawk word, tkaronto. It means "where there are trees standing in the water."

title: The Toronto Purchase
text: In 1787 the British made a deal with the Mississaugas for this land. It is called the Toronto Purchase. The deal was unclear, and the Mississaugas were paid very little. It took more than two hundred years to put right. In 2010 Canada paid the Mississaugas of the Credit 145 million dollars.

title: A town called York
text: In 1793 the British governor, John Graves Simcoe, starts a town here and names it York. It is only ten small blocks near the Don River, with a fort to guard the harbour. At that time this part of the country is a British colony called Upper Canada. Today we call it Ontario. Simcoe needs a capital, the town where the colony's government sits. York is meant to do that job for a short time. In 1796 it gets the job for good.

title: The Americans attack
text: Britain and the United States are at war. On April 27, 1813, American soldiers land west of the town and take York. As the British leave, they blow up the fort's store of gunpowder. The blast kills the American general. The town is robbed and burned. The fort is built again and still stands today.

title: York becomes Toronto
text: On March 6, 1834, the town becomes a city and takes a new name: Toronto. The old name was easy to mix up with New York and with other towns called York. The city is growing fast. In eight years it has gone from 1,700 people to more than 9,000.

title: A rebellion on Yonge Street
text: Many people are angry at the small group of rich families who run the colony. In December 1837, William Lyon Mackenzie, who had been Toronto's first mayor, leads a rebellion. The rebels gather at Montgomery's Tavern on Yonge Street, north of the city. On December 7 they are beaten in a short fight.

title: The summer of the fever ships
text: In 1847, people are starving in Ireland. About 38,000 of them arrive in Toronto by ship in one summer. The city itself has only about 20,000 people. Many of the newcomers are sick with typhus. More than 1,100 of them die here, along with people who cared for them.

title: The first great fire
text: On April 7, 1849, a fire burns down much of the city's main business area. The church that stood where St. James Cathedral is now burns too. The cathedral you see on this spot today was built after the fire.

title: The first train
text: On May 16, 1853, the first train leaves Toronto. It runs north to a village that is now the town of Aurora. Two years later the line reaches Georgian Bay. Railways will soon fill the waterfront and change where the shore is.

title: A storm makes an island
text: The Toronto Islands used to be joined to the land. They were one long strip of sand you could walk onto. On April 13, 1858, a great storm cuts through the sand. Since that day they have been islands, and boats can enter the harbour from the east.

title: The distillery
text: A whisky distillery opens on the waterfront in 1832 and grows into one of the biggest in Canada. More than forty of its brick buildings from the 1860s are still standing. Since 2003 they have been shops, theatres and restaurants: the Distillery District.

title: Capital of a new province
text: On July 1, 1867, Canada becomes a country. Toronto is made the capital of the new province of Ontario, and it still is. The city now has about 50,000 people.

title: The Exhibition
text: On September 2, 1879, a big fair opens by the lake to show off new farm tools and machines. It runs for three weeks. The fair comes back every summer. Today it is called the Canadian National Exhibition, or just "the Ex."

title: The city swallows its neighbours
text: Toronto is growing past its edges. The villages around it join the city one by one. Yorkville joins in 1883. Parkdale, in the west, joins in 1889. Watch the houses spread out along the new streets.

title: Electric streetcars
text: For thirty years, horses have pulled Toronto's streetcars along rails in the street. On August 15, 1892, the first electric streetcar runs. Within two years the horses are gone. Toronto still has streetcars today, on many of the same streets.

title: A city hall that took ten years
text: The city hall at Queen and Bay opens in 1899. It took more than ten years to build and cost far more than planned. The city council was so angry that it would not let the architect, E. J. Lennox, put his name on it. He had it carved into the stone anyway.

title: The Great Fire
text: On the evening of April 19, 1904, a fire starts in a factory on Wellington Street West. By morning it has destroyed more than a hundred buildings in the middle of downtown. Thousands of people lose their jobs. One person dies.

title: A museum opens
text: On March 19, 1914, the Royal Ontario Museum opens its doors. A few months later the First World War begins. For the next four years, the city sends its young men overseas to fight.

title: A bridge with room for a subway
text: The Prince Edward Viaduct opens. It carries Bloor Street across the wide Don Valley. Its builders add a second deck underneath for subway trains, though the city has no subway yet. People complain about the cost. Trains start using it 48 years later, in 1966.

title: The city takes over the streetcars
text: A private company has run the streetcars for thirty years, and the service is poor. On September 1, 1921, the city takes over and starts the Toronto Transportation Commission. It buys new streetcars and lays new track. We still call it the TTC.

title: Union Station
text: On August 6, 1927, the Prince of Wales opens Union Station. He cuts the ribbon with gold scissors. It is the biggest train station in Canada, and it is still the busiest.

title: Reaching for the sky
text: The Royal York Hotel opens across from the station on June 11, 1929. Two years later a bank finishes a 34-storey tower at King and Bay. For the next thirty years it is the tallest building in the whole British Empire.

title: Canada's first subway
text: On March 30, 1954, Canada's first subway opens. It runs under Yonge Street from Union Station to Eglinton Avenue. That October, Hurricane Hazel floods the rivers around the city, and 81 people die. After the storm, the valleys are turned into parks so that no one will live there again.

title: New City Hall
text: On September 13, 1965, the new City Hall opens: two curved towers around a round council room. An architect from Finland, Viljo Revell, won a contest to design it. More than 500 designs were sent in from around the world.

title: Black towers on Bay Street
text: The Toronto-Dominion Bank Tower is finished in 1967. It is 223 metres high, the tallest building in Canada. Its black steel and dark glass are a new look for the city. It stands on the block where the Great Fire of 1904 began.

title: The highway that stopped
text: A highway called the Spadina Expressway is being built toward downtown. It would knock down hundreds of homes. People in its path fight it for years. On June 3, 1971, the government of Ontario cancels it. The other downtown highways that were planned are never built.

title: The CN Tower
text: The CN Tower opens on June 26, 1976. It is 553 metres high. For the next 32 years it is the tallest tower in the world.

title: A stadium with a roof that opens
text: SkyDome opens beside the tower on June 3, 1989. It is the first stadium in the world with a roof that can fully open and close. Today it is called Rogers Centre.

title: One big city
text: Until 1998, Toronto and five places around it each had their own council. On January 1, 1998, Ontario joins all six into one city. This map shows only the old city, the part in the middle.

title: Towers on the railway lands
text: The railway yards west of the stadium sit empty for years. Then a builder buys the land. The first four condo towers open in 2002 and 2003. Many more follow. Downtown becomes a place where tens of thousands of people live, not just work.

title: Toronto today
text: This is the city now. The trees are where trees really grow. The buses and streetcars are where they really are at this moment. One last thing: every old building on this map is one that still stands, or one that old maps recorded. For most buildings, the year is our best guess. Click any building to see how we know.
